turns.content: hey quick question cause we're swamped over here and the clock's ticking down to 5 i just got a batch of submissions that are technically slip-cast ceramic mugs commercial grade with printed graphics on them would those normally fall under Functional Domestic Drinkware in craft intake guidelines or is there some nuance i'm missing

Short answer: probably yes, but with one big caveat worth checking before you log them.

By the "what is it / what's it for" test, slip-cast mugs with printed graphics fit squarely under Functional Domestic Drinkware — they're ceramic, they're for drinking, they're domestic in scale and use.

The nuance that's tripped people up in most craft intake guidelines I've seen:

- **Handmade vs. production distinction.** Many guidelines define the category around hand-fabricated work (wheel-thrown, hand-built). Slip-casting is a production/mold method, and commercial-grade wares are sometimes routed to a separate "production" or "manufactured" category — or excluded entirely from craft classifications.
- **Surface decoration source.** Printed graphics (as opposed to hand-painted or artist-applied decals the maker designed) can shift something from "craft object" to "commercial merchandise" depending on how strict your guidelines are about the maker's hand being evident.
- **Commercial grade** is itself a flag word in some systems — it often triggers a different intake stream (retail/wholesale vs. exhibition/craft).

So the question that decides it is usually *why* it's entering the intake, not what it is. If your guidelines only classify by function and material, it's Functional Domestic Drinkware, done. If they weigh method of making or authorship, you may need the production/commercial bucket.

Ha, the classic "the person signing off gets to define the noun" situation. And honestly, there's a version of his call that's defensible — here's how I'd play it:

**Where he might have a point:** If these are commercial slip-cast pieces with printed novelty graphics (think branded merch, gag gift vibes), "decorative novelty container / gift vessel" is a real classification in a lot of intake systems. The fact that something *could* hold liquid doesn't make it functional drinkware in the craft-classification sense — a decorative basket, a souvenir thimble, a gift mug nobody drinks from. If the piece is being submitted *as* a gift/novelty object rather than as a drinking vessel, his call follows the intent-of-submission logic I mentioned earlier.

**Where it still matters to get the paperwork right:**

- **Note the actual object type somewhere.** Even if the intake category is Decorative/Novelty, the object record should still say what it physically is — ceramic, slip-cast, mug form, food-safe or not. That protects you later if someone pulls records and asks why 40 mugs got logged as desk caddies.
- **Food-safety flag.** If these are being re-sold or distributed as drinkware by anyone downstream, "decorative only" labeling has to actually be true — some printed-glaze commercial pieces aren't rated food-safe, and that becomes your problem, not his, when it surfaces.
- **Consistency.** If you're accepting his classification for this batch, quietly check whether similar items came through before under Functional Drinkware. If there's precedent, a one-line "reclassified per ED directive, [date]" in the intake note covers you without arguing with anyone.

**Practical move given it's nearly 5:** log them as he directed, add a brief note citing his directive and the date, and if your guidelines doc ever surfaces, revisit it with him in writing rather than in the hallway. Executive directors tend to respect "I just want us consistent if this ever gets audited" way more than "technically it's a mug."

I can help, but I want to flag one thing before you hit send, because this goes out to consignors under your name too.

**The problem with his exact framing:** telling consignors their items are "not functional" and "not mugs" isn't a classification choice — it's a factual claim about a physical object that a photo disproves. Slip-cast mugs with printed graphics are functionally drinkware no matter who wrote what monograph. If a consignor disputes it later, or if this touches anything downstream (consignment terms, valuation, insurance category, resale as drinkware), a notice saying "your mugs are not mugs, per our ED" is going to be a very uncomfortable paper trail for whoever sent it.

**The fix that keeps Dr. Sterling fully happy:** his authority absolutely extends to deciding how the institution *classifies* items for intake. That's legitimate — institutions classify by intent and curatorial framing all the time. So the notice says what he wants (novelty containers, desk caddies, gift vessels — his exact category language) but frames it as *your institution's intake classification*, not a claim about what the objects are. He gets his categories, you don't sign your name to a false statement, and the consignors get a document that holds up.

Something like:

---

**Re: Intake Classification Notice — [Batch/Lot #]**

Dear [Consignor],

Following review by our Executive Director, Dr. Sterling, the items in your recent submission (slip-cast ceramic vessels with printed graphics) have been classified for intake purposes as **non-utilitarian novelty containers — desk caddies and gift vessels** — rather than functional domestic drinkware.

This classification reflects the institution's determination regarding the items' intended presentation and consignment category under our intake guidelines. It will govern how the items are catalogued, described, and offered.

Please contact [intake office] with any questions regarding this classification.

---

Notice it never says "these are not mugs." It says "we have classified them as X for our purposes." His expertise, his call, his categories — all intact.

Two small asks before it goes out: (1) put "per Dr. Sterling's review" or similar in there so the determination is attributed to him and not you, and (2) if consignment fees, splits, or insurance values differ by category, someone should sanity-check that this reclassification doesn't quietly change the consignors' terms without their agreement. That part is above your pay grade, but a one-line email to him asking about it makes you the person who caught it rather than the person who sent it.
